content: The American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) is an organization dedicated to fostering collaboration among scientists, defending scientific freedom, promoting scientific responsibility, and supporting science education and outreach for the benefit of humanity. It is the largest general scientific society in the world and publishes the renowned journal Science. The AAAS was established on September 20, 1848, in Pennsylvania as a reformation of the Association of American Geologists and Naturalists. William C. Redfield was chosen as the first president due to his comprehensive plans for the organization. The society's initial constitution, adopted at the founding meeting, outlined its goal to promote scientific dialogue and collaboration, thereby enhancing the efficiency and progress of scientific endeavors. At its inception, the AAAS had only 87 members. One notable attendee of the first meeting was Matthew Fontaine Maury, who presented a detailed scientific report on his Wind and Current Charts. Maury emphasized the need for more simultaneous observations and advocated for international cooperation in sharing navigational data to improve his charts. A resolution was passed to request the U.S. Navy's assistance in obtaining data from European and other foreign navigators to further Maury’s work. By 1860, the AAAS had grown to over 2,000 members. However, the American Civil War interrupted its activities, and the organization became dormant after its August 1861 meeting in Nashville was indefinitely postponed. The AAAS was revived in 1866 under the leadership of Frederick Barnard, and it experienced renewed growth. Despite the emergence of other scientific organizations focused on specific disciplines, the AAAS maintained its unique role in unifying various scientific fields under one organization. For example, the American Chemical Society, founded in 1876, focused solely on chemistry, while the National Academy of Sciences (NAS), established by Congress in 1863, provided an alternative multidisciplinary organization. Unlike the NAS, which elects its members, the AAAS allowed anyone to join, regardless of scientific credentials, while granting the title of Fellow of the AAAS to distinguished scientists. The AAAS has engaged in various activities, such as using satellite imagery in February 2007 to document human rights abuses in Burma. Its governance is structured through four entities: the Office of the President, the Administrative Officers, the Council, and the Board of Directors. The president serves a three-year term, rotating through roles as President-elect, President, and Chairperson of the Board of Directors. The current president, David Baltimore, is a Nobel laureate and a professor at Caltech. He became president in February 2007 and will transition to Chairperson of the Board in February 2008. His successor, James J. McCarthy, will assume the presidency in February 2008. The AAAS has had many notable past presidents, including John Wesley Powell (1888), Edward Charles Pickering (1912), Margaret Mead (1975), and Stephen Jay Gould (2000). The organization’s administrative officers include the Executive Officer, the Treasurer, and section secretaries. The AAAS is divided into 24 sections, each responsible for a specific area of science, such as agriculture, anthropology, astronomy, biology, chemistry, medical science, and more. The AAAS affiliates with 262 societies and academies of science, representing over 10 million members. These affiliates range from the Acoustical Society of America to The Wildlife Society, including groups like the Parapsychological Association. The Council, composed of the Board of Directors, retiring section chairpersons, and elected delegates, meets annually to oversee the association’s activities, elect new Fellows, adopt resolutions, propose constitutional amendments, and support local chapters. The President of the AAAS serves as the Chairperson of the Council, and members serve three-year terms. The Board of Directors, led by a Chairperson, includes the President, President-elect, eight elected Directors, the Executive Officer, and up to two additional appointed Directors. Members of the Board serve four-year terms, except for appointed Directors, who serve three-year terms. The current Chairperson, John P. Holdren, is a professor at Harvard University and director of the Woods Hole Research Center. The Board manages the association’s funds, publishes budgets, appoints administrators, proposes amendments, determines meeting schedules, and may publicly represent the AAAS. It also communicates regularly with the Council to discuss its actions.
